Thursday, the 16th March, 2000/ 26 Phalguna, 1921 (Saka) The House

OBITUARY REFERENCE 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow the passing 
away of Shri J.S. Raju, a former Member of this House, at the age of 65, in the 
early morning of 15th March, 2000. Born at Thirumanthurai in Tamil Nadu, 
in November, 1935, Shri Raju was educated at Pera mbalur and Trichy. An 
agriculturist by profession, Shri Raju started his career as a teacher. He was 
associated with several social welfare organisations. 
Shri Raju started his legislative career as a Member of the Tamil Nadu 
Legislative Assembly and was a Member in 1967 and re-elected again in 1971 
and 1980. He represented the State of Tamil Nadu in the Rajya Sabha from 
July, 1989 to July, 1995. During his tenure, he took keen interest in the 
deliberations of the House. He had a number of publications to his credit. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri J.S. Raju. 
I request the Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark 
of respect to the memory of the departed soul. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute) 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Secr etary-General will convey to the Members of the 
bereaved family our deep sense of sorrow and sympathy.

spite of substanital reduction in the poverty proportions was the rise in

below poverty line was achieved by a combination of accelerated rural growth 
and direct attack on poverty through anti poverty programmes. Substantial 
success has been achieved in containing the incidence of poverty and mitigating 
the severity of the poverty problem in the country. However, vigoro us efforts 
are needed to completely eradicate poverty from the country. 
(d) The Government has adopted a three pronged strategy for reducing  
poverty. It comprises of (i) accelerated economic growth with a focus on sectors 
which are employment intensive; (ii) human and social development through 
basic minimum services; and (iii) targetted anti -poverty programmes. There  
has been a growing recognition that successful implementation of the anti  
poverty programmes depends on the active participation of the benef iciaries 
in the formulation and execution of such programmes. The anti -poverty 
programmes for generation of both self -employment and wage -employment 
have, therefore, been recently redesigned to improve their efficacy/impact on  
the poor. Formation of self help groups is encouraged to bring forth the inherent 
potential of the poor to help themselves. The self help groups are assisted by  
the Government agencies by providing training, technical guidance and  
financial support to take up income generating activit ies that would enable  
the beneficiaries to earn a decent level of living.

2292. SHRI K.C. KONDAIAH: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be

(SHRI S.B.P.B.K SATYANARAYANA RAO): (a) As per EXIM policy the

commodities including Tur fixed by the Government are uniform for the whole

Soil Erosion 
2297. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that over 57 per cent of country's land 
area is suffering from various levels of degradation and that a staggering 5.3 
tonnes of top soil is lost every year through erosion; as reported in the Hindustan 
Time dated 10th February, 2000; 
(b) whether it is a fact that excessive use of the chemical fertilizers and 
over-exploitation of ground water resources have spell disaster in some States; 
and 
(c) if so, how Government propose to tackle this problem of soil conservation 
etc. and whether any study at central level is proposed to be undertaken? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI S.B.P.B.K. SATYANARAYANA RAO): (a) As per the assessment made 
by Indian Council of Agriculture Research (ICAR), out of the total geographical 
area of 329 m.ha, of the country, the area affected by soil degradation is about 
187 m.ha (57%) and approximately 5334 m tonnes of soil is lost per annum. 
(b) Yes Sir, in some states (list enclosed) (see below) the constant fall in 
groundwater level due to over exploitation is a matter of concern. As far as the 
level of fertilizer consumption in India is concerned, it is far below as compared 
to advanced countries like Netherland, U.K., Japan, etc. 
(c) Indian Council of Agriculture Research (ICAR) has generated data on 
nature and extent of Soil degradation in the country and worked out appropriate 
land use planning to prevent Soil degradation. Suitable mechnical, bio -
engineering measures and management practices to alleviate soil degradation 
problems have already been developed. 
The Department of Agriculture and Cooperation is implementing following 
Schemes to control the problem of land degradation in the country,  which 
indirectly help recharge the groundwater:—  
(i) Soil Conservation in the catchments of River Valley Projects and 
Flood Prone Rivers. 
(ii) Watershed Development Project in Shifting Cultivation Area. 
(iii) National Watershed Development Project in Rainfed Area. 
(iv) Reclamation of Alkali Soils.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI S.B.P.B.K. SATYANARAYANA RAO): (a) and (b) Under the existing 
scheme, Urea is the only fertilizer under the statutory price control. In the 
case of decontrolled Phosphatic and Potassic fertilizers like Di -Ammonium 
Phosphate (DAP), Muriate of Potash (MOP),  Single Super Phosphate (SSP) 
and Complex fertilizers, a scheme is in operation to provide concession to 
manufacturers and importers to enable them to sell these fertilizers at a reduced 
price indicated by Central/State Governments. 
Even with these concessions the average consumption of ferilizer nutrients 
(NPK) in India is about 90Kg/ha. The ferilizer use gives economic resonse 
and higher yields even at much higher doses of fertilizer application, hence, 
the present level can not be described as high or ex cessive.The nutrient 
consumption in Pakistan, in broadly identical situation is 113 Kg ./ha., in 
Bangladesh 135 Kg./ha. and in Sri Lanka 160 Kg/ha. The consumption in 
developed countries is much higher being 375 Kg./ha. In Japan, 542 Kg./ha. 
in Netherlands and 379 Kg/ha. in U.K. 
At this level of ferilizers consumption in India, there may not be any cause 
for concern to environmentalists. 
(c) and (d) Urea, which is the only controlled fertilizer is available to the 
farmers, including small and marginal farmers, at a subsidised statutory farm -
gate price. Decontolled fertilizer like DAP, MOP, SSP and complexes are also 
available to the fanners at concessional rates.

2315. SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that benefits of the research works conducted 
by various Agriculture Universities/Institutes have not reached the farmers;

71 

RAJYA SABHA [16 March, 2000] 
farmers and these universities to pass on the knowledge and expertise to the 
farmers; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (c) Government are aware 
with the importance of the benefit of the research works reaching the farmers. 
The Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) have been implementing 
various frontline extension programmes through the State Agricultural 
Universities (SAU), ICAR Institutes and other organizations. These are as 
follows:—  
(1) The Council have established 261 Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVK) 
including 13 9 with the SAUs. The activities of KVKs include on -
farm testing for identifying the technologies on location-specific basis, 
front- line demonstration to establish the production potentiality of 
technologies on farmers' fields, skill training of farmers and in-service 
training for extension personnel to update their knowledge. 
(2) The Council have sanctioned establishment of 40 Agricultural 
technology Information Centres (ATIC), including 25 in SAUs, to 
serve a single window system to provide solutions to the problems of 
the farmers and make available all technological information 
alongwith technology products for their testing and use 
(3) A project on Technology Assessment and Refinement through 
Institution Village Linkage Programme (IVLP) has been launched by 
the Council at 42 centres including 24 SAUs. The concept is based 
on participatory mode ensuring greater scientist -farmer linkage in a 
'bottom up' approach. 
Besides, all the State Agricultural Universities have their own 
Directorates of Extension to undertake various activities for 
dissemination of technology to the farmers, which include farm 
advisory services, training of farmers and inservice personnel, adaptive 
trials on farmers, fields, field days, front -line demonstrations, kisan 
melas, workshops, diagnostic services, special campaigns, publication 
of extension literatures and technical support to TV and Radio 
programmes.

2332. SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be

(a) whether Government are aware that many atomic power projects all 
over the world have resulted into serious radiation leakage even in developed 
countries;

accident and what was the outcome of such accident; and 
(c) whether Government have any plan to close all atomic power projects 
in the country like similar decision taken by many developed countries due to 
inherent risk of radiation in the environment? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF ATOMIC 
ENERGY (SHRIMATI VASUNDHRA RAJE): (a) Ever since nuclear power 
stations started operating in the 1950s, there were only two accidents world -
wide which led to serious leakage of radioactivity. The first one occ urred in 
1979 at the Three -Mile Island Nuclear Power Plant in the United States and 
the other one in 1986 at the Chernoby 1 Nuclear Power Plant in the erstwhile 
Soviet Union. These accidents were rated at level 5 and level 7 respectively as 
per the classification of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). IAEA 
classifies nuclear events into a scale of 1 to 7 in the International Nuclear 
Event Scale (INES). Levels 1 —3 are termed only incidents and levels 4 —7 
are termed accidents. The accident at Three- Mile Island resulted in severe 
damage to the reactor core. However, there was no loss of life and the off -site 
release of radioactivity was limited. The accident at Chernoby 1 had wide -
spread environmental and health impacts. Thirty-one people died in the course 
of the accident or soon after and another 137 were treated for acute radiation 
effects. 
(b) There has been no nuclear accident in Indian nuclear power plants ever 
since the first power reactor was commissioned at Tarapur in 1969. 
(c) No, Sir. There is no s uch plan. In fact, more nuclear power plants are 
currently under construction and commissioning.

eradicated only when the poor start contributing to the growth by their active

Assessment of GDP 
2439. SHRI S. RAMACHANDRAN PILLAI: 
SHRI E. BALANANDAN: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the cost of negative environmental impact of development is 
being taken into account while assessing Gross Domestic Product (GDP); 
(b) if not, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether Government are aware that over 10 per cent of the country's 
GDP is being lost annually due to environmental damage and related impact; 
(d) if so, the reaction of the Government thereto; and 
(e) the steps Government has taken to control the environmental damage? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING, 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STATISTICS AND 
PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION AND MINISTER OF STATE IN THE 
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND  PUBLIC 
GRIEVANCES OF THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, PUBLIC 
GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) No, Sir. 
(b) Though concerns have been expressed both at national and international 
levels to take into account the environmental damages in the econom ic 
aggregates, it has not, however, been possible to evolve firm agreement at the  
international level on concept, definition, measurement and valuation of  
environmental assets and degradation beyond natural rejuvenation process.  
Therefore, the UN Statistic al Commission has not recommended that the  
estimates of GDP be corrected for environmental damages. 
(c) and (d) No official estimates of the loss of GDP due to environment 
damage and related impact are available. Some research studies are, however, 
available which indicate such losses varying from 2.64% to about 10%. These 
research studies are not based on comparable methodology and are heavily 
influenced by the value judgement of research workers. 
(d) Several steps have been taken by the Government to prevent and control 
176 

[16 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
damage to the environment. Measures taken include prevention and control of 
pollution through legislation viz., Air (prevention and control of pollution) 
Act, 1981, Water (prevention and control of pollution) Act, 1974 as amended 
upto the 1988, Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, Forest (Conservation) 
Act, 1980, Bio-  Medical Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 1988, 
National Environment Tribunal Act, 1995, National Environment Appellate 
Authority Act, 1997, the E nvironment (protection) (Second Amendment) 
Rules, 1999— Emission Standards for New Generator Sets, Municipal Solid 
Wastes (Management and Handling) Rules, 1999 notification., etc; 
Mandatory Environment Impact Assessment of Development Projects to 
mitigate damage to Environment; Emphasis on Pollution Prevention rather 
than end of the Pipe Pollution Control; Fiscal incentives to the industries for 
adopting cleaner production technology; an allocation of Rs. 850 crores made 
for 2000- 2001 for implementing vario us schemes of the Ministry of 
Environment including Control of Pollution and Afforestation.

FAREWELL TO RETIRING MEMBERS 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, today we bid farewell to some 
of our colleagues who are retiring on the 2nd April, 2000, after completion of 
their term. Some, doubtless, will be re-elected while others will make way for 
new Members. The process of democratic renewal, so unique to the Rajya 
Sabha, will continue.Those who are retiring will, certainly, be missed by the 
House. Parting from one's colleagues brings sadness, which is but natural. 
When the House meets again, some familiar faces will be missing. I have no 
doubt, they will be missed as much by adversaries as by allies. The House is 
a special place where familiarity breeds affection, not contempt. 
As a Presiding Officer of this House, I shall, certainly, miss you - the 
passion of your arguments, the liveliness of your speeches; your temper and 
your laughter, your annoyance and your courtesy. If the House didn't have its 
moods, it shall be quite a boring place. Consistency is the virtue of dull 
assemblies. 
The membership of the Rajya Sabha is an intimately personal and 
intensely political experience. The hon. Members, who retire today, were the 
veterans whose contributions enhanced the stature of this House and helped 
mould public policy to subser ve larger causes. One of my enduring joys as 
Chairman was to watch adversaries bury their differences to uphold 
institutions. I have already considered it my duty to promote that 
understanding. I am glad, I never felt let-down in my labours. 
Many of these veterans retiring today, had mastered the art of debate 
and, even while taking digs at political opponents, remained civilized and 
decorous. I valued their help in maintaining the sanctity of the well of the 
House and, despite occasional aberrations, the i nviolability of the Question 
Hour. I believe that civilized debate is the finest form of communication that 
removes misunderstandings, promotes understanding and enables common 
good to transcend political, ideological and personal barriers. I am quite sure , 
when you look back on your life, at some distant date; or when you will speak 
to your grandchildren about your journey through life, your term in this House 
will, if I may use a familiar Parliamentary terminology receive a "special 
mention". You shall fe el proud of this chapter in your life's story. I know, 
those leaving this House on completion of their term will miss its special 
ambience, its unending excitement and will be marvelling, for a long time to 
come how, sitting in this precincts, they influenced the course of India's 
history.   I place on record my heartfelt appreciation of the valuable 
203 

RAJYA SABHA [16 March, 2000] 
contributions the retiring Members have made to the deliberations of the House, 
and the service they have rendered to Parliamentary democracy. Personally, I am 
grateful for the courtesy and consideration they have always shown me in 
conducting the business of the House. I wish them good health, happiness, success 
and long years of service to the nation. The House shall ever reme mber their 
association. 
THE LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION (DR. MANMOHAN 
SINGH): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I wish to associate myself with the noble 
sentiments that you had just now expressed on behalf of all the Members of this 
House. Ours is a democracy committed to the ideals of an open society, an open 
society trying to transform itself with in the framework of the rule of law. 
Parliament plays a very important role in facilitating that process of social and 
economic transformation. We live in a world where the only  constant thing is 
change itself. But ours is an unique institution -  Rajya Sabha -  change with 
continuity. Every two years, some Members retire, some fresh blood is introduced 
and that adds to the vitality of our institution, as reflected in the changing moods of 
our country; and that is as it should be. So, we will miss the absence of our 
colleagues who will be retiring today. Some of them have been stalwarts of our 
political life, but political life does not begin or end with Parliament. Our 
political system needs their guidance so that, collectively, we can work together 
to attain the cherished goals enshrined in our Constitution, to get rid of the 
chronic poverty, ignorance and disease which still afflict millions and millions of 
our countrymen and countrywomen. So, those of our colleagues who will not be 
coming back, 1 do hope that, at a later stage, they would be able to come back. 
But even those who are not coming back, I think they have a very important role to 
play in ensuring that politics in our country remains a purposeful instrument of 
social and economic change. We will rejoice when you come back and those 
who will not be coming back, I wish to say bon voyage. We will miss your 
absence, but you have an important task still to perform in our coun try, in the 
social and economic life, in a different capacity. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Shri E. Balanandan. He is not here. Dr. P. Alladi 
Rajkumar. He is also not here. Shri S. Viduthalai Virumbi. 
SHRI S. VIDUTHALAI VIRUMBI (Tamil Nadu): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I 
wish to associate myself, on behalf of the DMK party, in offering good wishes to 
the retiring Members.  Sir, the Leader of the Opposition just now

said that public life is not beginning or ending only with this august House. 
After having served for decades together in public life, our colleagues have 
entered here. Some of our elders paved the way for us to enter this august 
house. We also have to pave the way for the others to enter. But, at the same 
time, we have moved like a family. When some of our colleagues are retiring, 
we are genuinely feeling their departure. It is a natural feeling. Yet, it is 
unavoidable. We hope some of our friends come back again. Those, who do 
not, we hope, will come at least in the next elections. Eve n if they don't come 
back to this House, we hope they will be engaged in public service 
throughout their life. As Alfred had said, we are all working for one thing and, 
that is, welfare of the nation. Maybe, our strategies are different for achieving 
our a ims and ambitions: We may be aggressive sometimes; there may be 
acrimony sometimes because whatever takes places in the august House is 
mainly based on our convictions; but, when we come out in the Lobby, one 
can find us standing shoulder to shoulder, whic h in a way symbolises that the 
unity and the integrity of our nation is strong and our National Flag is flying 
high. I hope we will continue to get the services of our colleagues who are 
retiring from this august House and I also hope they will have a better life in 
future and that they will guide the future generations. With these words, 1 offer 
my good wishes and conclude my remarks.

SHRI PRAFULL GORADIA (Gujarat) : Mr. Chairman, Sir, may I shift to 
some hard-headed economics, after we have heard so much emotional poetry? Hon. 
Shri Dipankar Mukherjee referred to the voluntary retirement scheme earlier this 
morning, while discussing a question. He said, 'V.R.S'. Sir, I feel that not only 
are we retiring; at least, in my case, I am also getting a good golden hand-shake, 
as defined by Shri Ansari Sahib, again this morning. Of course, I am going, 
according to the law because as my trade union friends know very well, under the 
Industrial Disputes Act, the principle is, "Last come First Go; Last in First Out." I 
think I have the honour of obeying that law. I came here only 23 months ago and, 
therefore, I consider myself about the youngest Member of this august House. I 
assure you that the compensation, the VRS, that I have received, is both 
economical as well as emotianally satisfying. As far as economics is concerned, 
not that I am one myself, but there must be many hard-headed economists here in 
this House who will appreciate that the essence of economics is minimum of input 
and maximum of output. 1 think, in my case, it applies very appropriately because I 
came here not knowing how to speak in public. I had very limited political 
experience. This august House has given me in these 23 months a glorious 
opportunity at least to be able to stand up and say a few words. Before I came 
here, as far as I remember, every time I tried to speak, my knees would tremble and 
my voice would not come out. If my voice today is not clear because of my bad, 
sore throat, it is not because my knees are shaking. Therefore, economically, I 
have done well. I have learnt speaking in a very short time. 
I value a great deal the affection, which I have received. Over the last 
three or four days, something like 40 persons individually from different sections of 
the House have told me how much they will miss me. I never expected such 
affection, and I value the affection a great deal. My childhood was not an 
excitingly happy one. Therefore, I lap up very hungrily whatever affection I 
receive. Individually people have reassured me of their affection. 
I think I owe a great deal of gratitude to you, Mr. Chairman, Sir, the 
Deputy Chairman, the Vice-Chairmen on the Panel and others as well as my

I spoke, I cannot remember any occasion of a single speech having been

of speaking properly. 
For this, 1 owe you all, ladies and gentlemen, a great deal of 
gratitude. I shall remember these 23 months. I will cherish them, in fact, and 
will remember them as a bunch of very sweet memories. I take leave of all of 
you, wishing you all very good luck, happiness and health in your future 
years. I do not know whether 1 will ever get an opportunity to come back to 
this House. If I do, I will wish you again. I think it is easier to come in than to 
go out. 
I also salute the institutition of Rajya Sabha, and I am sure that it 
will remain a very sacred temple of our democracy. 
With this, I take leave. Good-bye, everyone.

RAJYA SABHA [16 March, 2000] 
nearly one-and-a-half hour to bid farewell to the retiring Members.. Anyway, 
I rise, today, really to bid my farewell to the great institution of Rajya Sabha 
and to express my deep gratitude to the Members, to the Ministers, to the 
Prime Minister, to the Leader of the House, to the Leader of the Opposition, 
for the undue indulgence that I might have received during my fifteen years' 
tenure in this House. Sir, anything which has a beginning is bound to have an 
end. That is why we are retiring on 2nd April, 2000. There has always been a 
practice of having a personal note on such occasion. I had travelled a long 
way in my life to reach this sacred place of Indian democracy, or, if I call it, 
the temple of democracy, or if I am  allowed to call it, the temple of learning. I 
joined the Communist Party at the age of 16. I had been in the militant 
students' movement in the 50s and 60s. I was a youth cadre. I am in the trade 
union. I worked and I am still working with the rural poor.  I must admit very 
frankly- and I don't feel that my Comrades will accuse me of Parliamentary 
deviations if I say so -  that my experience during all these vicissitudes of 
situation has been the most exciting in this august House of Rajya Sabha. It 
has alwa ys been rewarding. Parliamentary deliberations, Parliamentary 
discussions, opinions and counter opinions, in my opinion, reflect the basic 
contradiction within the society which, in our terminology, is called a class 
contradiction. May I very honestly and frankly say that this is an august 
House of Parliament? We have among us social activists. We have among us 
lawyers. We have among us industrialists and businessmen. We have among 
us political workers. But even today we do not have among us a single man or  
woman who is by profession a worker or who is by profession an agricultural 
worker in the country. This is, perhaps, unfortunately a serious limitation of 
Parliamentary democracy which the political parties should and must take into 
consideration. Parliament is really a place of learning. I have learnt to know 
my country more intimately after I joined Parliament in 1985. I have learnt to 
speak in the way I should. I have learnt to articulate. I have learnt to present 
my views during all these years of Parl iamentary deliberations. I thank all 
those who had interrupted me because their interruptions only inspired me to 
become a little more stronger and articulate in my understanding. Sir, what I 
have said is not an undue adulation of the system. This is a car dinal and most 
honest admission of the truth. While leaving Parliament I seek to pay my deep 
respect to my teacher, the Rajya Sabha, a national institution of Parliamentary 
democracy. I pay my respect to you, Sir, as the custodian of the wisdom of 
this House. We have no

[ 16 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
option but to strengthen the Parliamentary system. Whatever might be in the 
mind of those who would like to seek the revision of the Constitution or who 
would like to see that the present Constitution is totally changed or abrogated -
- I do not know what is in their mind- we have no option but to strengthen the 
Parliamentary system. We need a better Parliament. We need a good 
Parliament. We need effective Parliamentarians. We enjoy certain privileges 
and pe rquisites as Members of Parliament. We have to discharge our 
responsibility to the extent we are obligated to the system. If non -performing 
assets have been increasing enormously in the country and causing a great 
threat to the economy, Sir, non -performance in Parliament is also a grave 
danger to the Parliamentary system. The Indian political system, I must admit 
while leaving the House, has failed miserably even after 50 years of its 
existence. It has failed to ensure minimum human rights to a vast multitude 
of the people. The basic human problems have not been tackled by the 
politicians who had been in the corridors of power over the decades. Sir, the 
responsibility does not lie with one single Government. There is, I believe, an 
increasing impatience among the masses. The country is really at cross -roads. 
Violation of promise by those who came to power in successive Governments, 
wide gap between promise and performance, is a distinct feature of the 
disturbing political, economic and social conditions of th e country. Sir, as a 
Communist, I feel, Parliament has become an instrument for bringing about a 
social change, reflecting the mood and aspirations of the masses. If Parliament 
fails the way it had been, if Parliament does not pick up to rise to the occasion 
to meet the minimum requirements of national life, that will be a disaster; that 
will be a doomsday for Indian democracy. I believe that the masses of India 
will be on a move more energetically than they had been doing to put the 
political system on pro per rails. I should say, Sir, 'Long live Indian 
Parliament'; 'Long live Indian democracy'. I should say, while leaving 
Parliament, we remain in the mainstream of the political movement, allowing 
it to all to fight for a better India, to fight for a better life, to fight for a new 
future of the country. Keeping that in view, Sir, we are in the same boat - 
whether that side or this side, we are in the same boat -- maybe, the boat is 
being violently tossed in the turbulent sea of the Indian polity. But, we are in 
the same boat. We share the common responsibility of giving an expression to 
these traditions of the people of the country -  therein only, the functioning of 
Parliament will have its fulfilment; therein only, people will believe 
Parliament has been an effective system to bring about

STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER 
REGARDING HIS RECENT VISIT TO MAURITIUS 
MR. CHAIRMAN: We will now have state ment by the Prime 
Minister regarding his recent visit to Mauritius. 
THE PRIME MINISTER (SHRI ATAL BIHARI VAJPAYEE):As 
the House is aware, Mauritius and India have enjoyed a very close and 
traditional friendship. This has been continuously fostered through visits at 
the highest level. I was invited by Dr. Navinchandra Ramgoolam, the Prime 
Minister of Mauritius, to be the Chief Guest on the occasion of the first 
Independence Day celebrations in the new millennium. It is symbolic that 12 
March was chosen by th e leaders and people of Mauritius as their 
Independence Day to commemorate Mahatma Gandhi Dandi Salt March. 
230 

[16 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
This is testimony to their commitment to the values of Mahatma Gandhi and 
friendship with India. 
My visit from 1 0-12 March provided an opportunity to renew 
contacts at the highest level with Mauritius and to sustain the momentum in 
our special relationship which is deeply rooted in the strong foundation of 
linkages of religion, language, culture and our shared civilisational heritage. 
During my stay in Mauritius, I had meetings with the President, the 
Prime Minister and the Vice-President of Mauritius, as well as the Speaker of 
the Assembly and leaders of political parties. The talks further widened the 
deep understanding and commonality of approach on bilateral and 
international issues which characterises our relations. It has always been our 
endeavour to share our expertise and experience with the Government and 
people of Mauritius. During my visit, three agreements  on bilateral 
cooperation in the field of trade and commerce, information technology and 
supply of coastal surveillance equipment with a credit of US $ 9 million and a 
Memorandum of Understanding in the field of oceanography was signed. 
Through these agree ments, our cooperative ties in these important areas will 
be further strengthened. 
It was also announced during the visit that direct air links will be 
established between Port Louis and Chennai. This has been greatly 
appreciated by the people of Mauritius. 
During the visit, I had the opportunity to inaugurate the Indira 
Gandhi Centre for Indian Culture in Mauritius which has been set up with 
assistance from our Indian Council of Cultural Relations. This new complex 
will further boost our bilateral cultural exchanges. The Centre is also 
expected to become a hub for cultural activities for the benefit of the Indian 
community in this region. 
Along with Prime Minister Ramgoolam, I also had the privilege to 
lay the foundation of an educational -cum-cultural institution named after 
Gurudev Rabindra Nath Tagore at Hot village in the northern part of 
Mauritius. The Government of India would contribute US $ 1 million towards 
implementing this project. A civic reception was organised in my honour on 
this occasion. Reca lling our historic bonds, I assured the people of Mauritius 
that India will always stand by the people of Mauritius in their hour 
231 

RAJYA SABHA [ 16 March, 2000] 
of need. 
The visit helped to further cement our bilateral relations which are, 
indeed, a sh ining example of the close and deep mutual understanding 
between two countries. It would be the policy of the Government to continue 
to build upon this relationship in the future.

SHRI GOPALSINH G. SOLANKI (Gujarat) : Thank you, Sir. 
Before I say anything, first of all, I would like to congratulate Ms. Mamata 
Banerjee for being the first -ever wo man Railway Minister. Now, I am not 
going into the details of the Railway organisation, its expenditure, the number 
of employees working in it, the number of passengers, and the amount of 
freight carried by it. I am not going to discuss that aspect. 
First of all, I would like to invite the attention of the hon. Minister to 
accidents. In 1960 -61, the total accidents were 2,131. Of course, they are 
reducing year by year. However, during the last two years, the casualty has 
mounted like anything. In 1997-98, the casualty was more. 
I would also refer to the last two years' accidents, which have 
mounted like anything, more than 300 each. When accidents occur, we get 
information that an enquiry has been set up, but we get no result. Of course, 
some officers must h ave been punished. I want to say that more than 90 per 
cent of the railway accidents have occurred due to negligence of the staff, but 
no punishment is given to the staff that showed negligence in the performance 
of their duties. 
I am quoting the number of  persons died and the number of persons 
injured. In 1993-94, 179 persons died and 446 persons were injured. In 1997-
98, 1998-99 and 1999- 2000, deaths were 171, 280 and 328 and the persons 
injured were 747, 615 and 707 respectively. Of course, the hon. Mini ster may 
reply that there is a system of compensation under section 124 of the Railway 
Act. I will tell you what it is. In the case of death, the interim compensation 
that is paid to the next kin for death is just Rs. 15,000/ -; for grievous injuries, 
it is Rs.5,000/-, and Rs.500 for simple injuries. This is too less. As far as the 
interim relief is concerned, even according to the Motor Vehicles Act, the next 
of kin is paid Rs.20,000/ - for death, Rs.25,000/ - for grievous injuries and 
Rs.6,300/- for simple injuries. I would request the hon. Minister to amend this 
particular section so that the compensation is suitably enhanced. 
Moreover, there is one small lacuna. The compensation that is paid 
for death in case of accidents is not in consonance with the class  of journey 
provided by the Railways.   For death, something like Rs.l lakh or Rs.2.5

SHRI SHANKAR ROY CHOWDHURY (West Bengal): Mr. Vice -
Chairman, Sir, the Railway Budget for 2000 -2001 is the fourth Railway 
Budget in the series of the Railway Budgets during the 9th Five Year Plan 
from 1997-2002. The hon. Minister of Railways like her predecessors and, no 
doubt, like here successors has had to go through the annual process of trying 
to juggle with resources to produce something out of nothing. The biggest 
dilemma the Railway Minister faces is to present a people- friendly Budget 
vis-a-vis a railway friendly Budget. I must say that the Minister has done her 
best. She deserves our full support which she has. She also has my personal 
sympathies because this is a thankless task. The Railways have got to raise 
resources for the various project s that have been started prior to her and some 
which she has started. No doubt, due to various political as well as regional 
compulsions more such projects will be started. But, I think, we must stop and 
pause to see where the Railways themselves are going  because unless the 
Railways can strategically decide whether they are going to expand 
288 

[ 16 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
of whether they are going to consolidate, this problem will continue, not only 
in this Budget or this Five Year Plan but in the next Five Year Plan as well. 
I was not very well aware of the Fifteen -Year Plan which my hon. 
colleague spoke about. But I find a tremendous resemblance to the area where 
I had served - Defence Planning - and I note, both with happiness and sadness, 
that the Railways are also sailing in the same boat. So, what are the issues do 
we feel that the Railways should focus on? Firstly, from the strategic point of 
view, if you look at the overall railway map of India, the only two regions 
which are almost un- connected wi th the rest of the country through rail 
network, are Jammu and Kashmir and the North -East. Now, a very, very 
ambitious and a very, very expensive project from Jammu to Srinagar has 
been taken up. It is going along at a very slow pace. It is nobody's fault.  The 
terrain is very difficult. It is a major task and the resources, as always been, 
are short. Sir, an hon. Member from the North -East mentioned about the 
paucity of resources for the extreme North -East parts of our country. We must 
understand that the N orth-East and Jammu and Kashmir are strategic 
necessities for our country, and I do not know whether any Government, any 
Ministry, will have the necessary political will to ensure that resources are 
concentrated in these two major areas so that an overall railway network can 
be developed in these two extremities of our country as well. The other 
strategic area, which I think the Railways must focus on and which I find from 
the allotment of resources that they are not focussing on, is the process of 
electrification. I say that because the fossil fuels are fast running out. The 
sources of these fossil fuels are located in those regions of the world which 
are not under our control. Therefore, I do feel, as a strategic necessity for the 
country, we must focus on  electrification of the Railways to the maximum 
extent possible. We must allow time to the existing system to get more time 
for repairs, recuperation, rest and maintenance. I note from the figures that 
were given to us that, perhaps, out of the 62,000 kms.  of railway track, 
approximately, 11,000 kms. to 12,000 kms. of track is fully choked due to the 
frequency, of traffic, and the reminder of the railway network requires 
replacement. Will this Government or the succeeding Governments, either 
this year or ne xt year, have the courage, the political will, to reduce the 
number of trains so that whatever the existing frequency, whatever the 
existing network we have got, which is already in a bad shape, at least, gets 
time for adequate maintenance and repairs?

is why people love the Railways like  anything. More Members speak on 
Railways because they would like to see the Railways reaching to villages 
and the remotest areas. I appreciate the concern expressed by hon. Members. 
1 am very grateful to them. I know today is the last day. I can reply to all the 
questions put by the hon. members. But I do not want to waste the time of the 
House. That is why I would respond to a few suggestions which the hon. 
Members have made. I am grateful to Shri Bairagiji, who initiated this 
discussion. For Bairagiji's information, I would like to say that whatever he 
mentioned as lakhs, is not lakhs, it is crores. 
Please see the pink book. You will get all the figures. Bairagiji, you 
are a senior Member. If you feel that I have done something wrong with 
Madhya Pradesh, please let me know that. Whatever suggestions you have 
made, I will respond to all your suggestions. I will get back to you and give 
all the details. 
Sir, some points have been raised regarding commercial utilization 
of the land and that it might be misuse d. I would like to assure the House that 
the Railways is not going to sell the property anywhere. Railway land is our 
asset. It is the asset of the country. We want to utilize some railway land and 
some railway stations also as model stations. We want to u tilize some land 
and the air space for commercial purpose. At some places we would like to 
have a joint venture with the private sector. We are already having it with the 
public sector companies like HUDCO, IRCON and RITES. That is for 
development purposes only. Let me assure the House that we are not going to 
sell any property. There are 16 lakh employees in the Railways. They will get 
full protection. The Indian Railways is not going to be privatized. It is very 
much with the Government and it will remain with the Government. It is

only for the purpose of development. It has been sanctioned in the Ninth Five 
Year Plan. There is paucity of funds. Sir, we want to run the trains for the 
purpose of development. For that we need money. That is why there are some 
proposals for commercial utilization of land and air space. Of course, we will 
go in for commercial utilization of air space. Sir, development of the 
Railways means the development of the country. It is also eco nomic 
development of a particular State. I am not saying that we are encouraging the 
private sector. Let me clarify this point very specifically. If the State 
Government agrees to take up any new project, if the private sector agrees to 
participate in our development project, we will always welcome them. I 
would like to give an example. 
One MoU has been signed between the Railways and the Pipava,Port. 
There is one broad gauge line from Pipava Port to Surinder Nagar. They are 
spending one -third money and we are spending one -third money the 
remaining 1/3 money will be through borrowing. If any sector is prepared to 
invest money for connecting a port with the Railways, we will certainly 
welcome them. Sir, there is a need for reforms. We are going in for reforms . 
But without the help of people no reforms are possible. Without the help of 
the people our reforms cannot be successful. That is why we want to involve 
people everywhere. Instead of selling the property, we are going in for joint 
ventures. Let me assure the House very categorically. We have seen it earlier 
also. Now somebody was saying, "Have a Zonal Committee." Somebody else 
was saying, "Have a Divisional Committee." Somebody was saying, "Create 
more new Zones." Sir, there is a paucity of funds. We are f acing some 
difficulties. That is why this new Zone business is under review. Let me 
mention one thing. I feel that the time has come when we have to go in for 
decentralization. We have to decentralize the system. Our concept has to be 
changed. I feel that the States should be more powerful. If the State is 
powerful, the Centre is powerful. Instead of doing this type of business, I 
would prefer to set up a Monitoring Committee in every State to look after 
the project implementation from beginning to end. The re should be a 
Monitoring Committee in every State to look after the projects, to look after 
the development, to look after the implementation and specially to look after 
the problems of that particular State where the Railways is involved. We are 
going to announce it.   If there is a Monitoring Committee in every State, it

will help us a lot. Of course, sometimes, one Zone covers two States and 
sometimes it covers four States. Then, it is not possible for one State to hav e 
communications with another State. That is why, I think, the concept should 
be changed. The concept should be to reach the grassroot level so that we can 
have better monitoring, better coordination and all that. 
Regarding accidents, of course, the House has been expressing its 
concern, and I am also equally concerned about it. I do not know whether 
anybody would believe me or not, we, in the Railways, work 24 hours to 
ensure the safety aspect. There is a monitoring system and a coordination 
system for 24 hours, through which we see to it that no accident takes place. 
It is a fact that accidents, sometimes, take place. This is an unfortunate part of 
our system. But, is it not a fact that every day the Railways run 12,000 trains, 
and lakhs and lakhs of peopl e travel in these trains every day? Out of these 
12,000 trains, there are 7,000 passenger trains and 5,000 goods trains. And, 
when you take the case of road accidents, it accounts for 65,000 in a year. 
Yes, the Railway accidents are visible in nature. We w ant that no accident 
takes place. We do not want any human lives to be lost; we cannot 
compromise with human lives. But it is also a fact that the Railways have 
become the soft targets. If you have any political movement, then, the 
Railways is the target. If you have any extremist movement, then also, the 
Railways is the target. Political problems may be there in States. I don't say 
anything about it. We are in a democratic country. We have to appreciate this.

burn the bogies, and so on. When we have economic problems, we can invest 
our money for development purposes. In these four or five months, what we 
have done is - I am not saying that I alone did it; we work as a team --  that we 
convened a meeting with the GMs, not once but twice. We tried to ascertain 
whatever information and assistance they wanted. I should say that it is after a 
gap of 14 years that we have convened meetings with DRMs because it is 
they who are working with the grassroot people, and it is they who coordinate 
with various zones and divisions. In this very House, while we were 
discussing the Supplementary Demands, Shri Janardhana Poojary asked me:

being faced by the RP F and the GRP. This is a very important thing that we 
ought to have if at all we want to ensure

Disinvestment in Public Sector Units 
SHRI BRATIN SENGUPTA (West Bengal): Mr. Vice -Chairman, 
Sir, I would like to draw the attention of the Government to a very important 
318 

[16 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
issue, which has been agitating the minds of all sections of patriots, 
particularly the economists, planners, trade unions, workers and employees of 
this country. The subject is, disinvestment of public sector units. This process 
of selling out the prec ious public sector units had begun in 1991, concurring 
with the offensive of the liberalisation policy of the then Narsimha Rao 
Government and their Finance Minister, Dr. Manmohan Singh. At that point 
of time itself, most of the planners of our country, em inent economists, trade 
unions, many political parties, the Left parties in particular, employees, and 
many patriotic sections of the people and their forums had expressed alarm at 
this way of selling out the precious national assets of our country. From t he 
beginning, the target had not been the inconsequential public sector units, 
which were not accruing much profit to the exchequer of the Government, 
but the target had been the precious navratnas and 10 public sector 
undertakings, in particular, about which the entire nation has been feeling 
proud since independence. But, the Government did not care to any 
opposition, and any voice of protest since 1991. I am more concerned now. 
The issue has become very important now because the process of 
liberalisation and selling out of the precious public sector units has taken a 
further dangerous dimension with the unprecedented decision of the present 
Government to set up a separate department, that is, the Department of 
Disinvestment, after the disinvestment Commis sion of our country was 
allowed to be lapsed. As a result, an amount of almost 20,000 crores of 
rupees has already been allowed to be disinvested. There are many other 
units, like the Gas Authority of India, IPCL, etc. which are facing the threat 
of disinvestment, the policy which has already been framed by this particular 
department. This is a serious threat not only to our economy, not only to our 
national assets, but, I think, many of us will agree, cutting across the political 
affiliations, that this also is a serious threat to the economic sovereignty of our 
country. It is not a new thing that I am saying. Many political parties, 
including Members of the ruling party, at different points of time, at different 
occasions, have expressed this serious conce rn. But the Governments of the 
day have never cared to listen to them. They have been going on selling out 
this national asset. This threat to national sovereignty, or economic 
sovereignty, in particular, is a matter of serious concern, which, I feel, shou ld 
have been discussed long back in an elaborate manner on the floor of the 
House. I had also submitted a Calling Attention Motion on the subject, which 
has not yet been allowed. Therefore, I would request you, Mr Vice-Chairman, 
Sir, to impress upon the Minister to respond to the queries of

subject on the floor of the House. Without which, no Government would

has always tried to put forward on this aspect, which to me, and perhaps 
also to many other Members, and also to the people of this country, is not

starving, they are running short of funds, and that adequate funds are not

disinvest the precious public sector units in order to overcome your fiscal

This is a logic to divert the attention of the people  from the 
diktats that have been given to the Governments of the day in order to 
overcome our fiscal deficit. That is why the Government has resorted to 
this dangerous step. I will only seek your protection. Sir, the Government 
should not resort to this ty pe of tactics of diverting the basic issue, and try 
to convince the people in a wrong way that the funds from the 
disinvestments are going to the social sector, and that it is getting its due. 
The fact is that no services to the social sector have till now been rendered

of India. Again, I request you to impress upon the Government the need for 
a full-fledged discussion on the subject before proceeding further. Sir, this 
discussion should take place at the earliest convenience of the Rajya 
Sabha. With these words, Sir, I conclude.
